description: Citation-backed excerpts (verbatim or tight paraphrase, each <=80 words) from academic papers/reports on Noyyal/Bhavani textile-effluent impact on agriculture, Kalingarayan canal irrigation, Erode/Tiruppur powerloom-dyeing cluster labour, and turmeric price volatility.
source_title: (per-record citations below; each record carries its own source_url)

records.topic: Noyyal river textile-effluent impact on agriculture
records.citation: Rajkumar, A. Samuel and Nagan, S. (2010). 'Study on quality of effluent discharge by the Tiruppur textile dyeing units and its impact on river Noyyal, Tamil Nadu (India).' Journal of Environmental Science and Engineering, 52(4): 333-342.
records.excerpt: 729 textile dyeing units in Tiruppur discharged 96.1 million litres/day of wastewater into the Noyyal river. Even after common effluent treatment plants were installed, TDS (900-6600 mg/L) and chloride (230-2700 mg/L) in river water exceeded standards, and downstream Orathupalayam dam sediments accumulated chromium, copper, zinc and lead; groundwater and soil contamination in the basin remains unrestored.

records.topic: Kalingarayan canal / textile-effluent impact on agriculture
records.citation: Mohanakavitha, T., Shankar, K., Divahar, R., Meenambal, T. and Saravanan, R. (2019). 'Impact of industrial wastewater disposal on surface water bodies in Kalingarayan canal, Erode district, Tamil Nadu, India.' Archives of Agriculture and Environmental Science, 4(4): 379-387. DOI: 10.26832/24566632.2019.040403.
records.excerpt: The Kalingarayan canal, crossing the textile town of Erode, receives untreated/semi-treated effluent from tanneries, textile and dyeing units. The canal 'has helped to cultivate more than 6000 hectares'; contamination from polluting industries in Erode and Tirupur has reduced the cultivated area 'to 3000 hectares,' and yield on remaining farmland 'has decreased to a certain extent.'

records.topic: Kalingarayan canal irrigation / farmer adaptation to water scarcity
records.citation: Lannerstad, M. and Molden, D. (2009). 'Pumped Out: Basin Closure and Farmer Adaptations in the Bhavani Basin in Southern India.' Chapter 11 in Molle, F. and Wester, P. (eds), River Basins: Trajectories, Societies and Environments, pp. 238-256. International Water Management Institute / CABI Publishing.
records.excerpt: The 13th-century Kalingarayan weir on the Bhavani River serves about 4,800 ha. As supply tightened, 'several farmers have also turned to external surface water resources, and lift water into the command area from the Bhavani River or the Thadapalli or Kalingarayan canals,' some pumping canal water more than 7 km into the Lower Bhavani Project area.

records.citation: Carswell, Grace (2013). 'Dalits and local labour markets in rural India: experiences from the Tiruppur textile region in Tamil Nadu.' Transactions of the Institute of British Geographers, 38(2): 325-338. DOI: 10.1111/j.1475-5661.2012.00530.x.
records.excerpt_type: paraphrase from publisher abstract (full text paywalled)
records.excerpt: Comparing two villages near the Tiruppur textile cluster, the study finds labour-market segmentation among Dalits is not simply caste-based: some Dalits gained textile/export-market jobs while similarly-placed Dalits from a nearby village did not, because access depends more on each village's local social economy than on urban industry demand.
records.note: Full text is paywalled (HTTP 402); citation and abstract content were retrieved via publisher abstract page and search snippet, not the full article.

records.citation: Brindha, S. and Sundareswaran, T. (2019). 'A Study On The Functioning And Performance Of Power Loom Companies At Pallipalayam, Erode Dt, Tamilnadu, India.' Journal of Emerging Technologies and Innovative Research (JETIR), 6(1): 599-604.
records.excerpt: Surveying powerloom owners at Pallipalayam (Erode district), the study found most units run 10-15 looms producing lungi cloth via job weavers; owners typically spend Rs 15,000-20,000/month on electricity and Rs 10,000-30,000/month on labour wages; order-flow, finance and labour were the top factors limiting profit, and 95% of owners said they had not benefited from any government scheme.

records.citation: Prabha, S. Aruna, Palanichamy, N. Venkatesa, Murugananthi, D., Shivakumar, K.M., Kalpana, M. and Balakrishnan, M. (2025). 'Spicing up the major markets of turmeric in India.' Plant Science Today, Early Access. DOI: 10.14719/pst.6080.
records.excerpt: Using 14 years of data (2010-2023) from Erode (Tamil Nadu), Nizamabad (Telangana) and Sangli (Maharashtra), the study found an upward price trend in all major turmeric markets alongside cyclical behaviour lasting 2-4 years, with price slumps lasting longer than booms -- a risk to farmers' incomes that a Minimum Support Price could help offset.
